analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling individual stocks while in office.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2025 with no cosponsors, has sat in the House Administration Committee with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal ethics law to stop members of Congress and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, stock options, commodities, and similar investments while the member serves. It would still allow broad index funds, government retirement accounts, and Treasury bonds, and it would let members keep holdings they already own at the start of their term or place them in a qualified blind trust. Violators could face civil fines under existing ethics rules. The ban would not take effect until the start of the 120th Congress in January 2027 [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans get a Congress whose financial decisions are not entangled with the companies it regulates; members themselves gain a clear rule instead of reputational ambiguity.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding, purchasing, or selling individual securities, security futures, commodities, and synthetic economic interests like options and warrants during the member's term [S2].
Permits only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, the federal Thrift Savings Plan, and Treasury bills, notes, or bonds — investments that do not bet on specific companies [S2].
Subjects violations to civil fines under the existing ethics-fine framework in section 13106(a) of title 5 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest active trading in individual stocks, and financial firms that earn commissions on those trades.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers holdings: members may keep any individual stocks they already owned when their term began, so a member with a large pre-existing portfolio faces far fewer constraints [S2].
The ban does not begin until the first day of the 120th Congress in January 2027, leaving current members' trading governed only by existing disclosure rules for the rest of this Congress [S2].

Enforcement relies on the same civil fine system already on the books, which critics of congressional ethics rules have long considered weak; the bill adds no new enforcement agency or criminal penalty [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core restriction on trading individual stocks while in office is a real conflict-of-interest safeguard, and the allowed alternatives (index funds, TSP, Treasuries) leave members ample ways to invest. The grandfather clause and the delayed 2027 start date weaken it substantially — members could ride out their entire term on pre-existing stock positions — and the fine structure is the existing, modest one. A stronger bill would require divestiture rather than mere non-trading of prior holdings and would start sooner.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action; the committee has not scheduled a hearing or vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Bresnahan (R-PA) introduced the bill on May 5, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S1].
No cosponsors joined; the cosponsor list shows zero members [S3].
No committee action, markup, or floor vote has occurred since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, members of Congress themselves: with the bill parked in committee and no cosponsors, their ability to trade individual stocks remains governed only by existing disclosure rules, and the ban as written would not start until 2027 anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who can still trade stocks

for.name: Rep. Robert P. Bresnahan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban members of Congress and their spouses from trading individual stocks, and referred it to the House Administration Committee.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no markup, hearing, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes have been taken, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would bar them from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives during their terms, requiring them to use index funds, Treasury securities, or blind trusts. The grandfather clause lets them keep portfolios they already held, and enforcement is limited to civil fines under the existing system [S2].
A minor loss of trading business from roughly 535 households, mainly through lost commissions on congressional accounts.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since the May 2025 referral, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress. Stock-trading ban proposals have repeatedly stalled in committee despite public polling support, and this bill's single-sponsor, no-cosponsor status makes markup or a floor vote improbable before the committee's deadline pressure builds; the 2027 effective date further reduces urgency for the current membership.
